docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Infra Handbook

Working notes on Linux, cloud and infrastructure. Written while learning each topic hands-on, and kept as the reference I come back to.

$ tree infra-handbook
infra-handbook
├── linux/        16 chapters
├── bash/         3 chapters
├── aws/          next
├── terraform/    planned
├── docker/       planned
├── kubernetes/   planned
└── ci-cd/        planned
Revise one

Every chapter ends with interview points. Open one from the Linux section to start revising.

Show another

New here? Start with The Shell and use the Next link at the bottom of each page to read straight through.

docs.title: Bash Scripting
docs.text:
Writing scripts that are correct, readable and safe to run. Read in order.

  1. Bash Basics Arguments, command types, shebang, variables, expansion, arithmetic
  2. Conditionals, Loops & Functions Exit codes, && / ||, [[ ]], tests, loops, case, functions
  3. Script Safety set -euo pipefail, trap, mktemp, common pitfalls

docs.title: Bash Basics
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: Commands and arguments
docs.text:
• Bash splits a line on spaces → first word = command, rest = arguments
  • echo a b → 2 args → prints a b
  • echo "a b" → 1 arg → prints a b
  • Quotes decide how many arguments a command gets

docs.title: Types of commands
docs.text:
• Alias → text shortcut → ll = ls -alF
  • Function → named block of bash code
  • Builtin → inside bash itself → cd, echo, read
  • Keyword → bash syntax → if, for, while, [[
  • Executable → program file on disk → /usr/bin/ls
  • type cd / type -a ls → shows which kind
  • cd must be builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
  • Same name → alias wins, then keyword, function, builtin, executable

docs.title: [ needs spaces
docs.text:
• [ is a command → [ $x = 5 ] → args: $x, =, 5, ]
  • [$x = 5] → bash looks for command named [5 → not found

docs.title: Scripts and the shebang
docs.text:
• Shebang → #!/usr/bin/env bash → tells Linux which program reads the file
  • Without it → may run under sh, bash features break
  • .sh extension means nothing to Linux → first line decides
  • /usr/bin/env bash → finds bash in PATH → more portable than /bin/bash
  • Runnable needs → chmod +x + shebang → run with ./script.sh
  • ./script.sh → ./ needed because current dir is not in PATH
  • bash script.sh → shebang ignored, bash already chosen

docs.title: Special characters
docs.text:
• "..." → expands $var, keeps spaces
  • '...' → everything literal, no expansion
  • \ → escape next char
  • $ → expansion → $var, $(cmd), $((1+2))
  • # → comment
  • ; → run commands one after another
  • && → run next only if previous succeeded | || → run next only if previous failed
  • > < | → redirect, input, pipe (see Redirection & Pipes)
  • { } → group in same shell | ( ) → group in subshell
  • ~ → home | * → any chars | ? → one char

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
• name="aditya" → no spaces around =
  • "$name" → always quote
  • "${name}_bak" → braces when text touches the name

docs.title: Special parameters
docs.text:
• $0 → script name
  • $1 $2 → arguments
  • $# → number of arguments
  • "$@" → all args, each kept separate → use this
  • "$*" → all args glued into one string → only for messages
  • $? → exit code of last command, 0 = success
  • $$ → PID of current shell

docs.title: Parameter expansion
docs.text:
• ${var:-default} → default if empty/unset → PORT=${PORT:-8080}
  • ${#var} → length
  • ${f%.gz} → remove from end → backup.tar.gz → backup.tar
  • ${f#backup.} → remove from start → backup.tar.gz → tar.gz

Quoting danger

  • file='no secret'; rm $file → runs rm no secret → deletes wrong file
  • rm "$file" → one argument → correct

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
• Variables are strings by default → a=5; a+=2 → 52 (string append)
  • a=$((a + 2)) → 7
  • let a+=2 → 7
  • declare -i a=5; a+=2 → 7 → integer attribute, every assignment is math
  • a=5+2 → "5+2" text | declare -i a=5+2 → 7
  • Prefer $(( )) and (( )) → a=$((a+2)), (( a++ ))

docs.title: Here documents
docs.text:
• cat > file <<'EOF' ... EOF → write many lines into a file at once
  • Quoted 'EOF' → no expansion inside → $vars written literally
cat > notes.txt <<'EOF'
line one
$HOME stays as text
EOF

Interview points

  • Shebang purpose → picks the interpreter → #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash in PATH
  • $@ vs $* → "$@" keeps each arg separate, "$*" glues them into one string
  • Why is cd a builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
  • a=5; a+=2 gives 52 → variables are strings → use $(( )) for math

docs.title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
• Every command returns 0–255 → 0 = success, else failure
  • echo $? → see last exit code
  • exit 1 in scripts when something goes wrong
  • Exit codes are 0–255 → ping: 0 reply, 1 no reply, 2 other error
  • >&2 → send message to stderr → all error messages go there
  • ! cmd → flips exit status → ! grep -q bad file
  • grep -q → no output, just exit code → used in conditions

docs.title: && and ||
docs.text:
• mkdir d && cd d → cd only if mkdir worked
  • cd "$dir" || { echo "no dir" >&2; exit 1; } → stop script if cd fails
  • { ...; } groups commands → needs ; before }
  • ; vs && → ; runs next always, && only on success
  • a && b && c || d → d runs if ANY earlier one failed → group: a && { b || d; }

docs.title: if
docs.text:
• if [[ cond ]]; then ... elif [[ cond ]]; then ... else ... fi
if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
    echo "exists"
elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then
    echo "is a dir"
else
    echo "missing"
fi

docs.title: [ vs [[
docs.text:
• [ → command, unquoted vars get split → breaks on spaces/empty
  • [[ → bash keyword, no splitting → safe, supports patterns + regex
  • In bash scripts always use [[ ]]
  • [ apple < banana ] → < is redirection → use [[ ]] or \<

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Files → -e exists | -f file | -d dir | -r readable | -w writable | -x executable | -s not empty
  • -h file → true if symlink
  • f1 -nt f2 → f1 newer | -ot → older
  • [[ $var ]] → true if var not empty | [[ ! $var ]] → true if empty
  • Strings → -z empty | -n not empty | = != compare
  • Numbers → -eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge → or (( n > 5 ))
  • Strings vs numbers → "314" < "9" as text, but 314 -gt 9 as numbers
  • [[ $f == *.log ]] → pattern
  • [[ $u =~ ^[a-z]+$ ]] → regex
  • [[ $x = $pat ]] unquoted right side → pattern match | "$pat" quoted → exact string

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
• for f in *.log; do ...; done → loop files → never $(ls)
  • for i in {1..5}; do ...; done
  • for (( i=0; i<5; i++ )) → C-style loop
  • while read -r line; do ...; done < file → read line by line
  • read -r → don't treat \ as escape → always use -r
  • until cmd → loop while cmd fails → same as while ! cmd
  • break → exit loop | continue → next iteration
  • select → simple menu → rarely used

docs.title: case
docs.text:
• case $1 in start) ... ;; stop) ... ;; *) usage ;; esac
  • ;& → fall through to next block
case $1 in
    start) echo "starting" ;;
    stop)  echo "stopping" ;;
    *)     echo "usage: $0 start|stop" ;;
esac

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• name() { ...; }
  • Inside function → $1 $@ are the function's args
  • local var=x → variable stays inside function
  • return 0/1 → function exit code | exit → ends whole script

Interview points

  • [ vs [[ → [ is a command with word splitting, [[ is a keyword without it
  • a && b || c → c also runs if b fails → not a real if/else
  • return vs exit → return ends the function, exit ends the whole script
  • Why never for f in $(ls) → filenames with spaces split → use for f in *

docs.title: Script Safety
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: set -euo pipefail
docs.text:
• -e → stop when a command fails
  • -u → error on unset variable → stops $dirr typo becoming rm -rf /*
  • ${3:-} → empty if $3 missing → stops set -u from erroring on optional args
  • -o pipefail → pipe fails if any part fails, not just last
  • -e doesn't catch failures inside if or before && || → safety net, not guarantee

docs.title: trap
docs.text:
• trap 'cleanup' EXIT → runs when script ends, even on failure
  • Used to delete temp files / half-written archives

docs.title: mktemp
docs.text:
• mktemp → unique temp file | mktemp -d → temp dir
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmp"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

tar -czf "$tmp/backup.tar.gz" "$HOME/notes"

docs.title: Pitfalls 1–5
docs.text:
• for f in $(ls) → use for f in *
  • cp $file $dst → cp -- "$file" "$dst"
  • Filenames starting with - → use -- or ./*
  • [ $foo = bar ] → quote or use [[ ]]
  • cd $dir → cd "$dir" || exit 1
  • All the same rule → quote vars, globs not ls, handle failures

Interview points

  • set -euo pipefail flag by flag → -e stop on failure, -u error on unset var, -o pipefail pipe fails if any part fails
  • Does set -e catch everything → no, not inside if or before && || → safety net, not guarantee
  • trap cleanup EXIT → cleanup runs even when the script fails
  • Common bash pitfalls → quote vars, globs not ls, handle failures

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Based on The Linux Command Line by William Shotts. The notes are my own.

Shell and system fundamentals for day-to-day ops work. The chapters are in reading order, and each one links to the next.

  1. The Shell Shell vs terminal, the prompt, first commands
  2. Navigation The filesystem tree, cd, absolute and relative paths
  3. Exploring the System ls, reading files, key directories, symlinks
  4. Files & Directories Wildcards, cp, mv, rm, hard and soft links
  5. Working with Commands type, which, getting help, aliases
  6. Redirection & Pipes Streams, 2>&1, tee, filters
  7. Expansion & Quoting Globbing, braces, $(...), quoting rules
  8. Keyboard Shortcuts Line editing, history, job control keys
  9. Permissions chmod, chown, umask, special bits, sudo
  10. Processes ps, top, process states, signals, jobs
  11. systemd & Services systemctl, unit files, start vs enable, journalctl
  12. vi / vim Modes, editing, search and replace
  13. Package Management apt, dpkg, packages in Dockerfiles
  14. Networking IPs, routes, ports, DNS, curl, SSH
  15. Finding Files locate, find tests and actions
  16. Archiving & Backup tar, gzip, rsync, archive vs compress

docs.title: Archiving & Backup
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 18

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
• Archive → bundle many files into one, keeps perms/owners/timestamps → tar
  • Compress → shrink one file → gzip, bzip2, xz
  • .tar.gz → archive then compress → standard on Linux
  • zip → does both but loses Unix perms/ownership → avoid for Linux backups
  • Use cases → backups, deploys, moving data between servers

docs.title: tar
docs.text:
• Flags → c create | x extract | t list | f filename next | z gzip | v verbose | C extract into dir
  • tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/ → create
  • tar -tzf backup.tar.gz → list without extracting
  • tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp/ → extract into /tmp
  • tar rf a.tar file → append → only plain .tar, not .tar.gz
  • bzip2 / xz → smaller, slower → tar j = bzip2, tar J = xz
  • Leading / stripped on create → paths inside archive start home/me/... → check with tar tf
  • tar xf a.tar --wildcards 'home/me/dir-*/file-A' → extract only matching paths → quote so shell doesn't expand *
  • find dir -name 'file-A' -exec tar rf a.tar '{}' '+' → add found files → + runs tar once, \; once per file (see Finding Files)

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
• gzip file → file.gz, original deleted → gzip -k keeps it
  • gunzip file.gz → back → zcat / zless to view without extracting
  • gzip -l file.gz → compressed vs original size
  • Works on single files only → gzip dir/ fails

docs.title: rsync
docs.text:
• Syncs src → dest, copies only new/changed files → compares size + mtime
  • Over network sends only changed blocks → fast reruns, resumes broken transfers
  • rsync -av src/ dest/ → a = recursive + keep perms/times, v = verbose
  • rsync -avn → dry run
  • rsync -av --delete → exact mirror, removes extras in dest
  • rsync -av src/ user@host:/backup/ → over SSH
  • src/ → copies contents | src → copies the folder itself

Quick revision

  • tar -czf create | tar -tzf list | tar -xzf ... -C dir extract
  • rsync -avn first, then run for real → add --delete only for an exact mirror

Interview points

  • Archive vs compress → tar bundles, gzip shrinks, zip loses Unix metadata
  • rsync vs scp → scp copies everything every time, rsync only changes + resumes
  • rsync src/ vs rsync src → trailing slash copies contents, no slash copies the folder itself

docs.title: Exploring the System
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 3

docs.title: ls options
docs.text:
• ls → Lists files and directories.
  • ls -l → Long listing: permissions, links, owner, group, size, modification time.
  • ls -a → All files, including hidden ones (. prefix).
  • ls -la → Long listing + hidden files.
  • ls -h → Human-readable sizes (K, M, G); use with -l → ls -lh.
  • ls -t → Sort by modification time (newest first).
  • ls -r → Reverse the sort order.
  • ls -S → Sort by size.
  • ls -ld dir → Info about the directory itself, not its contents.
  • Options combine: ls -lth → long, newest first, readable sizes.

docs.title: Reading a long listing
docs.text:
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 3576 Apr 1 10:00 file.txt
  • - → file type (- file, d directory, l symlink)
  • rw-r--r-- → permissions: owner / group / others
  • 1 → number of hard links
  • root root → owner, group
  • 3576 → size in bytes
  • Apr 1 10:00 → last modified
  • file.txt → name

docs.title: Viewing File Content
docs.text:
• cat file → Displays the complete contents of a file.
  • less file → Views a file page by page; good for large files.
    • /word search, n next match, G end, g start, q quit
  • head file → First 10 lines by default (head -n 20 file for 20).
  • tail file → Last 10 lines by default; tail -f file follows a live log.

docs.title: File Information
docs.text:
• file filename → Determines the file type (Linux ignores extensions).
  • wc file → Counts lines, words, and bytes (wc -l lines only).
  • du -sh dir → Disk usage of a directory, human-readable.
  • df -h → Free/used space per filesystem, human-readable.

docs.title: Key directories
docs.text:
• / → root of everything
  • /etc → system config files
  • /var/log → logs
  • /home → users' home dirs; /root → root's home
  • /bin, /usr/bin → programs; /sbin → admin programs
  • /tmp → temp files, cleared on reboot
  • /proc → live kernel/process info (virtual, not on disk)
  • /dev → device files
  • /opt → third-party software
  • /boot → kernel + bootloader

docs.title: Symbolic links (symlinks)
docs.text:
• A symlink = a shortcut / a note that points to another file or folder.
  • It holds no content, only the path to the target.
  • ls -l shows it as l at the start and link -> target.
  • Delete the target → the link breaks ("No such file or directory").

docs.title: Creating and replacing links
docs.text:
• ln -s target link → create a new symlink
  • ln -sf target link → replace an existing link to a file (-f = force)
  • ln -sfn target link → replace an existing link to a folder
    • (-n = treat the link itself, don't follow it into the folder)
  • -sfn is safe for files too, so it can be used for every replacement.

docs.title: Real examples on Ubuntu
docs.text:
• /etc/localtime -> /usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Kolkata → timezone
  • /usr/bin/python3 -> python3.12 → version switch
  • /bin -> usr/bin → whole folder is a link

docs.title: DevOps use: deploys and rollbacks
docs.text:
• /app/current -> /app/releases/v2; the server always runs from /app/current
  • Deploy: ln -sfn /app/releases/v3 /app/current
  • Rollback: ln -sfn /app/releases/v2 /app/current (instant)

docs.title: Files & Directories
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 4

docs.title: Wildcards (work with any command)
docs.text:
• * → any characters *.log → all .log files
  • ? → exactly one character file?.txt → file1.txt, fileA.txt
  • [abc] → one of these file[12].txt → file1.txt, file2.txt
  • {a,b} → each of these *.{log,md} → all .log and .md files
  • Test a wildcard safely first: ls *.log before rm *.log

docs.title: Creating
docs.text:
• touch file.txt → Creates an empty file or updates its timestamps.
  • mkdir dir → Creates a directory.
  • mkdir dir1 dir2 → Creates several at once.
  • mkdir -p dir1/dir2 → Creates parent directories if they don't exist.

docs.title: Copying
docs.text:
• cp source destination → Copies a file.
  • cp -r source_dir destination_dir → Recursively copies a directory and its contents.
  • cp -i → Asks before overwriting.
  • cp -v → Shows what is being copied.
  • cp -a → Archive: keeps permissions, owner, timestamps (use for backups).

docs.title: Moving & Renaming
docs.text:
• mv source destination → Moves a file/directory.
  • mv old.txt new.txt → Renames a file.
  • mv file.txt /tmp/ → Moves a file to another directory.
  • mv -i → Asks before overwriting.
  • mv is used for both moving and renaming.

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
• rm file.txt → Removes a file.
  • rm -i file.txt → Asks before deleting.
  • rm -r directory → Recursively removes a directory and its contents.
  • rmdir directory → Removes an empty directory only.
  • rm -f file.txt → Forcefully removes a file without prompting.
  • rm -rf directory → Forcefully and recursively removes a directory.
  • rm permanently removes files; there is no recycle bin.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Inode → the number identifying where a file's data actually lives; see it with ls -li.
  • Hard link → ln file hardlink
    • A second name for the same data (same inode number).
    • Deleting the original does not delete the data; it's gone only when the last name is removed.
    • Can't point to a directory or across disks/filesystems.
  • Soft (symbolic) link → ln -s file softlink
    • A note pointing to the file's name (its own inode).
    • Breaks if the original is deleted.
    • Can point to directories and across disks.
  • ln -sfn target link → replace an existing link to a folder.

docs.title: Related (other chapters)
docs.text:
• find → Searches for files/directories based on criteria (ch 17).
  • locate → Searches for files using a pre-built database (ch 17).
  • which command → Shows the executable path of a command (ch 5).

Interview points

  • cp → Copy | mv → Move/Rename | rm → Remove
  • mkdir → Create directory | touch → Create file / update timestamps
  • find → Search filesystem
  • Hard vs soft link: hard shares the inode and survives deleting the original; soft has its own inode, can cross disks and point to dirs, and breaks if the target is deleted.

rm -rf

rm -rf is powerful and dangerous. In production, always verify the path before executing it (run ls on the same path first).

docs.title: Finding Files
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 17

docs.title: locate
docs.text:
• locate passwd → fast search by name from a database
  • Database updated daily → misses new files → sudo updatedb to refresh
  • locate -i → case-insensitive
  • Use → quick "where is this file" | find → anything precise or recent

docs.title: find Basics
docs.text:
• find [where] [tests] [action] → e.g. find /var/log -name "*.log" -delete
  • No path → searches current dir | / → whole system → add 2>/dev/null
  • Always quote wildcards → find . -name "*.log" → else shell expands * first (ch 7)
  • Stacked tests = AND → find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" -size +10M

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• -name "*.log" → by name | -iname → case-insensitive
  • -type f → file | d → dir | l → symlink
  • -size +100M → bigger than | -size -1k → smaller than | units k, M, G
  • -mtime -1 → modified in last 1 day | +7 → older than 7 days
  • -mmin -30 → modified in last 30 min
  • -user ganesh | -group devs → by owner
  • -empty → empty files/dirs
  • -perm 777 → exact mode → find world-writable files (security check)
  • -maxdepth 1 → don't go into subdirs

docs.title: Operators (rarely needed)
docs.text:
• -o → OR | ! → NOT | \( \) → grouping
  • find . \( -name "*.log" -o -name "*.tmp" \) → logs or tmp files
  • find . -type f ! -name "*.md" → files that aren't markdown

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• -print → default, prints path
  • -delete → delete matches → run without -delete first to check
  • -exec cmd {} \; → run cmd once per file → {} = the file
  • -exec cmd {} + → run cmd once with all files → faster
  • -ok cmd {} \; → like -exec but asks before each
  • find . -name "*.sh" | xargs chmod +x → same idea via xargs
  • -print0 | xargs -0 → handles spaces in filenames

docs.title: Real Use
docs.text:
• find / -type f -size +500M 2>/dev/null → what's eating disk
  • find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete → clean logs older than 7 days
  • find ~ -type f -mtime -1 → files changed today
  • find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null → SUID binaries (security audit)
  • find . -name "*.conf" -exec grep -l "port" {} + → conf files containing "port"

Interview points

  • Disk full, find big files → find / -type f -size +100M 2>/dev/null or du -sh /* | sort -h
  • Delete logs older than 7 days → find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete
  • -exec {} \; vs {} + → once per file vs once with all files
  • locate vs find → locate = fast but stale db, find = live search

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 8

docs.title: Cursor Movement
docs.text:
• Ctrl-A → start of line
  • Ctrl-E → end of line
  • Alt-F / Alt-B → forward / back one word
  • Ctrl-L → clear screen (same as clear)

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
• Ctrl-U → delete everything before the cursor
  • Ctrl-K → delete everything after the cursor
  • Ctrl-W → delete the previous word
  • Alt-D → delete the next word
  • Ctrl-Y → paste back what was just deleted
  • Ctrl-_ → undo

docs.title: Completion
docs.text:
• Tab → complete a command, file or path
  • Tab Tab → show all possible completions
  • Works for commands, paths, ~user, $VAR, and (with bash-completion) git/kubectl/terraform subcommands

docs.title: History
docs.text:
• history → list past commands; history | grep docker → search them
  • ↑ / ↓ → previous / next command
  • Ctrl-R → reverse search; type part of a command, Ctrl-R again for older matches, Enter to run, Ctrl-G to cancel
  • !! → rerun the last command. sudo !! → rerun it with sudo
  • !$ → last argument of the previous command. mkdir logs && cd !$
  • Alt-. → paste the last argument (press again for older ones)
  • !n → run history entry number n. !git → last command starting with git
  • History file → ~/.bash_history (size set by HISTSIZE in ~/.bashrc)

docs.title: Process Control
docs.text:
• Ctrl-C → kill the running command (SIGINT)
  • Ctrl-Z → pause it (SIGTSTP); fg resumes, bg runs it in background
  • Ctrl-D → end of input; exits the shell if the line is empty

Quick revision

  • Ctrl-A/E start/end | Ctrl-U/K delete before/after | Ctrl-W delete word
  • Ctrl-R search history | !! last command | !$ / Alt-. last argument
  • Tab Tab completions | Ctrl-C kill | Ctrl-Z pause | Ctrl-L clear

Interview points

  • Ctrl-C sends SIGINT (stop); Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP (pause, resumable with fg).
  • sudo !! → fastest fix for "Permission denied".
  • Never put passwords or tokens on the command line; they're saved in ~/.bash_history.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 2

  • Navigation → Moving through the Linux filesystem hierarchy using shell commands.
  • Linux uses a hierarchical filesystem with / as the root directory.

docs.title: Important Commands
docs.text:
• pwd → Print Working Directory; displays the current directory.
  • ls → Lists files and directories in the current directory.
  • ls -la → Lists all files, including hidden files, with detailed information.
  • cd → Change Directory; moves to another directory.
  • cd .. → Moves to the parent directory.
  • cd ~ or just cd → Moves to the user's home directory.
  • cd - → Moves back to the previous directory.
  • cd / → Moves to the root directory.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
• Absolute path → Full path starting from /.
    • Example: /home/aditya/Documents
  • Relative path → Path relative to the current working directory.
    • Example: Documents/file.txt
  • . → Current directory.
  • .. → Parent directory.
  • ~ → Current user's home directory.

docs.title: Filename rules
docs.text:
• Hidden files start with . (e.g. .bashrc); plain ls doesn't show them.
  • Filenames are case-sensitive: File1 ≠ file1.
  • Avoid spaces in names; use _ or -.
  • Extensions don't matter to Linux; .txt is just part of the name.

Interview point

Absolute paths are independent of the current working directory; relative paths depend on it.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 16

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• IP address → device's address on a network → e.g. 192.168.1.9/24
  • /24 (CIDR) → first 24 bits = network → 192.168.1.0–255 is one subnet
  • Gateway → router that forwards traffic leaving your subnet → e.g. 192.168.1.1
  • DNS → name to IP → google.com → 142.250.x.x
  • Port → which service on a host → 22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 5432 Postgres

docs.title: Interfaces + Routes
docs.text:
• ip a → all interfaces + IPs (replaces ifconfig)
  • lo → loopback 127.0.0.1 | eno1 → ethernet | wlo1 → wifi | virbr0 → KVM bridge | CloudflareWARP → VPN tunnel
  • state UP/DOWN, NO-CARRIER → no cable | dynamic → IP from DHCP
  • ip r → routing table → default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlo1 = everything else goes to router

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
• ping host → ICMP echo, checks host is up + latency → ttl, time=ms, packet loss
  • ping can fail even if host is up → ICMP blocked by firewall/cloud security group
  • traceroute host → every hop to host (UDP probes by default)
  • * * * in a hop → hop not replying (blocked/VPN) → try sudo traceroute -I (ICMP) or -T -p 443 (TCP)
  • mtr host → live ping + traceroute combined

docs.title: Ports + Sockets
docs.text:
• ss -tulpn → listening ports → t tcp, u udp, l listening, p process, n numeric
  • ss -tulpn | grep :80 → who is on port 80
  • lsof -i :80 → same, via lsof
  • 0.0.0.0:80 → listening on all interfaces | 127.0.0.1:80 → local only, not reachable from outside

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
• resolvectl query urmilabs.com → DNS lookup via systemd-resolved
  • dig urmilabs.com +short → just the IP (sudo apt install dnsutils)
  • /etc/hosts → local name overrides, checked before DNS
  • /etc/resolv.conf → which DNS server is used

docs.title: HTTP Clients
docs.text:
• curl https://site → GET, prints body
  • curl -I → headers only → status code, server: cloudflare
  • curl -v → verbose → DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake, request/response
  • curl -L → follow redirects | -o file → save to file | -s → silent
  • curl -X POST -d 'k=v' url → send data (APIs, Telegram bot)
  • wget url → download file | wget -c → resume

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
• ssh user@host → encrypted remote shell | ssh -p 2222 → custom port
  • ssh -i ~/.ssh/key user@host → use specific private key
  • ssh-keygen -t ed25519 → creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) + id_ed25519.pub (public)
  • ssh-copy-id user@host → appends pubkey to remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  • Public key → goes on server | Private key → never leaves your machine
  • Permissions → ~/.ssh 700, private key 600, authorized_keys 600 → else "Permissions are too open" / key ignored
  • ssh host 'df -h' → run one command remotely
  • /etc/ssh/sshd_config → server side → PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no → restart sshd after change
  • ~/.ssh/known_hosts → fingerprints of servers seen → "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" = host key changed → ssh-keygen -R host
  • ~/.ssh/config → then just ssh sshlab:
Host sshlab
    HostName localhost
    Port 2222
    User root
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/sshlab

docs.title: File Transfer
docs.text:
• scp file user@host:/path → copy to remote | scp user@host:/path . → copy from remote | -r for dirs
  • sftp user@host → interactive transfer (put, get, ls)
  • rsync -avz src/ user@host:/dst → incremental sync, better than scp for big/repeat copies
  • ftp → plaintext, insecure, skip

Interview points

  • Can't reach a server → ping (up?) → ss on server (listening?) → firewall/security group → DNS (resolvectl/dig)
  • App works on server but not from outside → bound to 127.0.0.1 not 0.0.0.0, or port blocked
  • "Permissions are too open" → chmod 600 key, chmod 700 ~/.ssh
  • Ping fails but curl works → ICMP blocked, host is fine

docs.title: Package Management
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 14

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Package → archive with program files + metadata (version, deps, scripts) → Debian/Ubuntu use .deb
  • Repository → server hosting packages → listed in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/
  • Dependency → package needs another to work → apt resolves automatically
  • Two levels → apt (high: repos + deps) | dpkg (low: local .deb, no dep resolution)

docs.title: Find + Inspect
docs.text:
• apt update → refresh package index only, installs nothing
  • apt search nginx → search repos by name/desc
  • apt show nginx → version, deps, size before install
  • apt list --installed | wc -l → count installed pkgs
  • apt list --upgradable → what has updates
  • apt-cache depends htop → what htop needs
  • apt-cache rdepends --installed libc6 → what needs libc6

docs.title: Install + Remove
docs.text:
• sudo apt install -y htop → install from repo (-y = no prompt)
  • sudo dpkg -i file.deb → install local .deb → then sudo apt -f install to fix missing deps
  • sudo apt upgrade → install newer versions of installed pkgs
  • sudo apt remove htop → remove binary, keep config files
  • sudo apt purge htop → remove binary + config
  • sudo apt autoremove → delete deps no longer needed

docs.title: Query dpkg
docs.text:
• dpkg -l | grep htop → is it installed (ii = installed, rc = removed but config left)
  • dpkg -L htop → list every file the pkg installed
  • dpkg -S $(which ls) → which pkg owns a file → e.g. coreutils: /usr/bin/ls

docs.title: Docker / Scripts
docs.text:
• apt-get (not apt) in scripts/Dockerfiles → stable output for scripts
  • One layer, smaller image:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Interview points

  • update vs upgrade → update = refresh list, upgrade = install new versions
  • remove vs purge → purge also deletes config
  • "Unable to locate package" → run apt update, check spelling, check repo enabled
  • "Which package gave me this file?" → dpkg -S /path

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 9

  • Permissions → control who can read, write or execute a file or directory.
  • 3 classes → u owner | g group | o others | a all
  • 3 permissions → r = 4 | w = 2 | x = 1

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• id → your UID, GID and groups. id ganesh
  • groups → groups you belong to
  • whoami → current username
  • /etc/passwd → user accounts (no passwords) | /etc/shadow → hashed passwords (root only) | /etc/group → groups
  • New group membership applies after logout/login (or newgrp group).

docs.title: Reading ls -l
docs.text:
• -rwxr-xr-- 1 ganesh devs 220 Oct 28 script.sh
  • type | owner | group | others | links | owner | group | size | date | name
  • Type → - file | d directory | l symlink | c/b character/block device | s socket | p pipe

docs.title: Files vs Directories
docs.text:
• File → r read contents | w change contents | x run it
  • Dir → r list names | w create/delete/rename entries | x enter (cd) and access files inside
  • Dir r without x → can see names but not open anything.
  • Dir w needs x too to actually create or delete.
  • Deleting a file needs w on the DIRECTORY, not the file. You can delete a read-only file in your own folder.

docs.title: Octal
docs.text:
• 7 rwx | 6 rw- | 5 r-x | 4 r-- | 3 -wx | 2 -w- | 1 --x | 0 ---
  • 755 → rwxr-xr-x → scripts, directories
  • 644 → rw-r--r-- → normal files
  • 700 → rwx------ → private directory
  • 600 → rw------- → secrets, SSH private keys, .env files
  • 777 → everyone can write. Almost never correct.

docs.title: chmod
docs.text:
• chmod 755 f → octal
  • chmod u+x f | chmod g-w f | chmod o=r f | chmod a+x f → symbolic (+ add, - remove, = set exactly)
  • chmod u=rwx,go=rx f → several classes at once
  • chmod -R 755 dir → recursive (careful: makes every file executable)
  • stat f → shows permissions in both forms (e.g. 0644/-rw-r--r--)

docs.title: chown / chgrp
docs.text:
• sudo chown aditya f → change owner
  • sudo chown aditya:devs f → owner and group | sudo chown :devs f → group only
  • sudo chgrp devs f → group only
  • -R → recursive
  • Only root can change a file's owner.

docs.title: umask
docs.text:
• Sets the default permissions for new files and directories.
  • Base → file 666 | dir 777 (new files never get x by default)
  • umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755 (Ubuntu default)
  • umask 077 → files 600, dirs 700 (private)
  • It's a mask that REMOVES bits, not subtraction: umask 033 → files 644 (not 633)
  • umask alone shows the current value; set it in ~/.bashrc to make it permanent.

docs.title: Special Bits
docs.text:
• setuid → 4000, chmod u+s f → program runs as the FILE'S OWNER. /usr/bin/passwd (-rwsr-xr-x) runs as root so you can edit /etc/shadow.
  • setgid → 2000, chmod g+s → on a program: runs as the file's group. On a DIRECTORY: new files inherit the directory's group (shared team folders).
  • sticky → 1000, chmod +t dir → in that directory, only a file's owner (or root) can delete it. /tmp → drwxrwxrwt
  • chmod 2770 /srv/shared → setgid + rwxrwx---
  • Lowercase s/t → bit set AND x set | uppercase S/T → bit set but x missing (usually a mistake)
  • setuid is ignored on shell scripts (security).
  • find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null → list all setuid files (security audit)

docs.title: sudo / su
docs.text:
• sudo cmd → run one command as root; asks for YOUR password.
  • sudo -l → what you're allowed to run | sudo -i → root shell
  • sudo -u alice cmd → run as another user
  • Rules live in /etc/sudoers; edit only with sudo visudo (checks syntax, so you can't lock yourself out)
  • su user → switch user; asks for THAT user's password
  • su - user → full login shell (their env and home) | su - → root
  • passwd → change your password | sudo passwd alice → set someone else's

Quick revision

  • r=4 w=2 x=1 | u g o a
  • 755 scripts/dirs | 644 files | 600 secrets | 777 never
  • chmod permissions | chown owner | chgrp group | umask defaults
  • setuid 4 runs as owner | setgid 2 inherits group | sticky 1 only owner deletes
  • sudo your password | su their password

Interview points

  • "Permission denied running ./script.sh" → check x bit (ls -l), chmod +x; run bash script.sh to bypass; check if the disk is mounted noexec.
  • Even root can't run a file with no x bit at all; root can read/write anything.
  • SSH says "permissions are too open" → chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, chmod 700 ~/.ssh.
  • Deleting a file is controlled by the directory's w, not the file's.
  • Directory x = permission to enter/access; r = permission to list names.
  • /tmp is 1777: everyone writes, sticky bit stops users deleting each other's files.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 10

  • Process → a running instance of a program. vim file.txt → vim becomes a process.
  • PID → unique process ID | PPID → parent's PID
  • PID 1 → systemd on Ubuntu; starts and manages services; adopts orphaned processes.
  • /proc/<PID>/ → kernel's live info about each process (cat /proc/1234/status)

docs.title: Viewing Processes
docs.text:
• ps → processes in the current shell
  • ps x → all your processes, including ones with no terminal
  • ps aux → all processes, all users (BSD style)
  • ps -ef → same, but shows PPID (System V style)
  • ps aux --sort=-%mem | head → top memory users | --sort=-%cpu → top CPU users
  • Columns to read → USER, PID, %CPU, %MEM, STAT, COMMAND
  • ps aux | grep nginx → also shows the grep itself; pgrep -a nginx is cleaner.
  • pstree → parent/child tree | pstree -p → with PIDs

docs.title: top / htop
docs.text:
• top → live view of processes, CPU, memory, load. q quits.
  • Inside top → M sort by memory | P sort by CPU | k kill a PID | 1 show each CPU
  • Load average → 3 numbers = 1, 5, 15 min. Compare with CPU count (nproc): load 4 on 4 CPUs = fully busy.
  • htop → friendlier, colour, scrolling. sudo apt install htop

docs.title: Process States (STAT column)
docs.text:
• R → running | S → sleeping (waiting for something) | T → stopped (Ctrl-Z)
  • D → uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on disk/network; even kill -9 can't stop it.
  • Z → zombie: finished, but the parent hasn't collected its exit status.
  • Can't kill a zombie (it's already dead) → fix or restart its parent; once the parent dies, PID 1 cleans it up.
  • Orphan → parent died while the child is still running; PID 1 adopts it.

docs.title: Foreground / Background
docs.text:
• cmd & → run in the background. sleep 100 & → prints [1] 4321 (job number, PID)
  • Ctrl-Z → pause the foreground job
  • bg / bg %1 → resume it in the background
  • fg / fg %1 → bring it to the foreground
  • jobs → list jobs in this shell (jobs -l adds PIDs)
  • Background jobs die when the terminal closes (SIGHUP).
  • nohup cmd & → keeps running after logout (output → nohup.out) | disown → detach an already-running job

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
• kill sends a SIGNAL; it doesn't always mean "kill".
  • kill PID → SIGTERM (15): polite request; program can clean up and save.
  • kill -9 PID → SIGKILL (9): kernel removes it instantly; can't be caught or ignored; no cleanup.
  • kill -1 PID → SIGHUP: many daemons (nginx) reload their config on it.
  • Ctrl-C → SIGINT (2) | Ctrl-Z → SIGTSTP (pause)
  • kill -STOP PID / kill -CONT PID → pause / resume any process
  • kill -l → list all signals
  • Right order → kill PID, wait a few seconds, then kill -9 only if it's still alive.

docs.title: Kill by Name
docs.text:
• pgrep nginx → PIDs by name | pgrep -a → with full command | pgrep -u ganesh → by user
  • pkill nginx → signal all matching processes (careful: matches partial names)
  • killall nginx → same, exact name match

docs.title: Which process holds a port
docs.text:
• sudo ss -tlnp → listening ports with the process using each
  • sudo lsof -i :80 → what's using port 80

Quick revision

  • ps aux / ps -ef snapshot | top live | pgrep find | pstree tree
  • & background | Ctrl-Z pause | bg / fg resume | jobs list | nohup survive logout
  • kill TERM 15 | kill -9 KILL | kill -1 HUP reload | Ctrl-C INT 2
  • R run | S sleep | D disk wait | T stopped | Z zombie

Interview points

  • SIGTERM vs SIGKILL → TERM lets the program clean up (close files, release locks, finish writes); KILL can't be caught, so data or locks can be left broken. Always TERM first.
  • Zombie → finished process whose parent hasn't read its exit status. kill -9 does nothing; deal with the parent.
  • D state process won't die even with kill -9 → it's stuck on I/O (often a disk or NFS issue).
  • "Server is slow" → top (load average, CPU vs nproc, memory, swap) → sort by P/M → ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head → check that process's logs.
  • "Port 8080 already in use" → sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080 → find the PID → kill it or stop its service.
  • PID 1 is systemd; it starts services and adopts orphans.

docs.title: Redirection & Pipes
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 6

  • Redirection → Changes where a command's input, output, or errors go.
  • The shell sets it up before the command runs; the command never knows.

docs.title: 3 standard streams
docs.text:
• 0 stdin → input (keyboard)
  • 1 stdout → normal output (terminal)
  • 2 stderr → error messages (terminal)

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• > → stdout to file, overwrites (creates if missing). ls > out.txt
  • >> → stdout to file, appends. echo hi >> out.txt
  • > file → empties the file (clear a log).
  • Shell truncates BEFORE the command runs: sort f > f leaves f EMPTY.
  • set -o noclobber → blocks overwriting; >| forces it.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• 2> → stderr to file. find / -name x 2> err.log
  • 2>> → stderr to file, appends.
  • Split → cmd > out.log 2> err.log

docs.title: Both together
docs.text:
• 2>&1 → 2 stderr, > send to, &1 wherever stdout points RIGHT NOW.
  • & = "1 is a stream, not a file". 2>1 creates a file named 1.
  • By default 1 and 2 both point at the screen (terminal).
  • 2>&1 copies stdout's current destination once; it doesn't follow it later (like copying an address before someone moves house).
  • cmd > f 2>&1 → 1 moves to f, then 2 copies it → both in file ✅
  • cmd 2>&1 > f → 2 copies screen, then 1 moves to f → errors on screen ❌
  • Rule: put 2>&1 LAST.
  • &> / &>> → Bash shorthand for both (overwrite / append). Fails in sh/dash (cron); portable form is > f 2>&1.

docs.title: /dev/null
docs.text:
• Discards everything written to it.
  • cmd 2> /dev/null → hide errors | cmd > /dev/null 2>&1 → hide everything (cron)

docs.title: Input
docs.text: • < → stdin from file. wc -l < f → count only, no filename.

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
• | → stdout of one = stdin of next. Both run at the same time. ls | grep .txt
  • stderr is NOT piped → cmd 2>&1 | grep err or cmd |& grep err

docs.title: tee
docs.text:
• tee → writes to screen AND file. ls | tee out.txt (-a appends)
  • sudo echo x > /etc/f → Permission denied; echo x | sudo tee /etc/f → works.
  • Why: > runs as YOU before sudo starts; tee opens the file itself, as root.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
• cat a b > c → join files
  • sort → -n numeric, -r reverse, -rn largest first
  • uniq → removes ADJACENT duplicates (sort first); -c counts, -d only dupes
  • wc -l → lines (-w words, -c bytes)
  • grep x → matching lines; -v non-matching, -i ignore case
  • head -n 5 / tail -n 5 → first / last 5; tail -f log → follow live
  • Top 5 lines → sort f | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
  • Top 5 IPs → awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

Interview points

  • Redirection is set up by the shell before the command starts.
  • Pipe connects stdout → stdin; stderr needs 2>&1.
  • > f 2>&1 works, 2>&1 > f doesn't (left to right).
  • sudo echo > /etc/f fails; use | sudo tee.
  • Never redirect into the file you're reading.

docs.title: The Shell
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 1

  • Shell → a command-line interpreter that sits between the user and the Linux OS.
  • It interprets commands, executes programs, and manages redirection, pipes, variables and scripting.
  • The shell asks the kernel (through system calls) to start programs; the programs do the actual work.
  • Terminal → application/interface used to access a shell.
  • Terminal emulator → GUI app that gives you a terminal (gnome-terminal, Konsole).

docs.title: Shell ≠ Terminal
docs.text:
• Terminal → provides the interface
  • Shell → interprets and executes commands

docs.title: Common shells
docs.text:
• Bash → Bourne Again Shell (Ubuntu default)
  • Zsh
  • Fish
  • sh

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text:
• user@host:dir$ → standard bash prompt
  • $ → normal user | # → root

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• ↑ / ↓ → command history (bash keeps ~1000 by default)
  • date → current date/time
  • cal → calendar
  • df -h → disk free space
  • free -h → memory usage
  • exit or Ctrl-D → ends the session

docs.title: Expansion & Quoting
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 7

  • Expansion → The shell rewrites your command BEFORE running it. The program only sees the result.
  • echo shows what a command expands to → echo *.txt
  • Order → brace → tilde → parameter, command, arithmetic → word splitting → pathname (glob)

docs.title: Pathname Expansion (Globbing)
docs.text:
• * → zero or more characters. ls *.txt
  • ? → exactly one character. ls file?.txt
  • [abc] → one character from the set. ls file[123].txt
  • [a-z] / [0-9] → one character from a range.
  • [!abc] → one character NOT in the set.
  • [[:digit:]] [[:upper:]] [[:alpha:]] → character classes.
  • Done by the shell, not the command: ls *.txt runs as ls a.txt b.txt.
  • * skips hidden files (dotfiles); .* matches them.
  • No match → the pattern stays as plain text. ls *.xyz → ls: cannot access '*.xyz'

docs.title: Tilde Expansion
docs.text:
• ~ → your home directory. cd ~
  • ~user → that user's home. cd ~ganesh
  • Not expanded inside quotes: echo "~" prints ~.

docs.title: Brace Expansion
docs.text:
• {a,b,c} → makes one word per item. echo file{1,2,3} → file1 file2 file3
  • {1..5} → sequence. echo {1..5} → 1 2 3 4 5
  • {a..e}, {01..10} (zero-padded), {1..10..2} (step 2)
  • Real use → mkdir -p proj/{src,docs,tests} | cp app.conf{,.bak} → backup copy
  • Not a glob: creates names whether or not files exist.

docs.title: Parameter Expansion
docs.text:
• $name → value of the variable. name="Aditya"; echo $name
  • ${name} → explicit form; needed next to text. echo ${name}_logs
  • $name_logs → looks for a variable called name_logs (empty).
  • printenv / set → list variables.

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
• $(cmd) → replaced by the command's output. echo "Today is $(date)"
  • `cmd` → old syntax; $(...) preferred (nests, easier to read).
  • Real use → kill $(pgrep sleep) | cd $(dirname $(which python3))

docs.title: Arithmetic Expansion
docs.text:
• $((expr)) → integer maths. echo $((5 + 3)) → 8
  • Operators → + - * / % **
  • Integers only: $((5 / 2)) → 2 (no decimals; use bc for those).
  • Variables need no $ inside: x=4; echo $((x * 2))

docs.title: Word Splitting
docs.text:
• Unquoted expansions are split on spaces/tabs/newlines into separate words.
  • f="my file.txt"; rm $f → tries to delete my and file.txt ❌
  • rm "$f" → deletes my file.txt ✅
  • Rule: always quote variables → "$var"

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text:
• Double quotes "..." → stop word splitting and globbing; $, $( ), $(( )) and \ still work.
    • echo "$HOME has *" → /home/ganesh has *
  • Single quotes '...' → stop ALL expansion; everything is literal.
    • echo '$HOME has *' → $HOME has *
  • \ → escapes one character. echo \$HOME → $HOME | rm my\ file.txt
  • \ inside double quotes only escapes $, `, ", \ and newline.
  • Can't put ' inside single quotes; use "it's" instead.

Quick revision

  • * any | ? one | [abc] set | [!abc] not set
  • ~ home | {a,b} list | {1..5} sequence
  • $var / ${var} value | $(cmd) output | $((...)) integer maths
  • "..." expands $ only | '...' nothing expands | \ one character

Interview points

  • The shell expands the command first; the program never sees *, ~ or $var.
  • Globbing is done by the shell → why find . -name *.txt breaks; quote it: find . -name "*.txt"
  • Single vs double quotes: single = fully literal, double = variables still expand.
  • Always quote variables ("$var") to avoid word splitting on spaces.
  • Brace expansion makes names; globbing matches existing files.

docs.title: systemd & Services
docs.text: Hands-on notes, written while building and breaking a custom service

docs.title: What
docs.text:
• Service (daemon) → program running in the background, no window → e.g. cron, cups, NetworkManager, warp-svc
  • systemd → first program Linux starts at boot (PID 1) → manager of all services
  • Job → start services at boot, restart them if they crash, stop them at shutdown, log what happens
  • ps -p 1 → shows systemd as PID 1
  • systemctl → command to talk to systemd

docs.title: See services
docs.text:
• systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running → all running services
  • systemctl status cron → how one service is doing
  • Read status → Loaded: card found + enabled/disabled | Active: running/dead/failed → ignore the rest
  • ● running | ○ stopped | × failed
  • Main PID → process number of the service | CGroup → all processes belonging to it
  • Bottom lines → journal (systemd's diary for that service)
  • --no-pager → print fully, no scroll screen | -l → don't cut long lines

docs.title: Unit file (the card)
docs.text:
• Text file telling systemd how to run a service → ends in .service
  • systemctl cat cron → view a service's card
  • /etc/systemd/system/ → your cards | /usr/lib/systemd/system/ → package cards, don't edit
  • [Unit] → what it is → Description=
  • [Service] → how to run it → ExecStart=/path/to/program (the exact command systemd runs) | Restart=on-failure (restart if it crashes)
  • [Install] → when to start → WantedBy=multi-user.target (normal boot)
  • e.g. cups → ExecStart=/usr/sbin/cupsd -l → systemd runs that command for you

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
• sudo systemctl start x → run now
  • sudo systemctl stop x → kill it now
  • sudo systemctl restart x → stop + start → new PID
  • sudo systemctl enable x → start at every boot
  • sudo systemctl disable x → don't start at boot
  • sudo systemctl enable --now x → run now + at boot
  • systemctl is-active x | is-enabled x → quick yes/no checks

docs.title: start vs enable
docs.text:
• Two separate switches → now (start/stop) | boot (enable/disable)
  • start only → running now, gone after reboot
  • enable only → not running now, starts after reboot
  • disable cups → is-enabled = disabled, is-active = active → still running
  • enable → creates a symlink in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/ pointing to the card
  • disable → deletes that symlink, the card stays
  • .wants folder = boot list → systemd starts everything linked there at boot
  • WantedBy= in [Install] → tells enable which boot list → missing = "no installation config" error

docs.title: Lab: write your own service
docs.text:
A service that writes the date to a log every 10 seconds.

1. The script → /usr/local/bin/ticker.sh, then sudo chmod +x it

#!/bin/bash
while true; do
  date >> /tmp/ticker.log
  sleep 10
done

2. The card → /etc/systemd/system/ticker.service

[Unit]
Description=Ticker: append the date to /tmp/ticker.log every 10s

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ticker.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

3. Load and start it

sudo systemctl daemon-reload        # re-read cards; needed after every new or edited card
sudo systemctl enable --now ticker  # "Created symlink" = added to the boot list
systemctl status ticker             # active (running)
tail -f /tmp/ticker.log             # new line every 10s

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
• journalctl -u x → all logs for service x
  • journalctl -u x -n 20 --no-pager → last 20 lines
  • journalctl -u x -f → follow live
  • journalctl -p err -b → all errors since boot
  • Don't read every line → look for failed / error / No such file

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix bad-setting, "no ExecStart", "no installation config" [Unit] / [Service] / [Install] headers missing from the card Add the section headers, daemon-reload × failed with status=203/EXEC systemd couldn't run ExecStart: wrong path (tickr.sh, kicker.sh) or script not executable Fix the path, chmod +x, daemon-reload "Start request repeated too quickly" Restart= retried 5 times and gave up Fix the cause, daemon-reload, reset-failed x, restart x status=0/SUCCESS Not an error: clean exit Nothing to fix

docs.title: Debug order
docs.text:
1. systemctl status x → Active line + ExecStart path + last log lines
  2. journalctl -u x -n 50 --no-pager → more detail
  3. Edited the card? → daemon-reload + restart
  4. Check the ExecStart file exists and is executable → ls -l /path

Interview points

  • What happens on systemctl start x → systemd reads x.service, starts dependencies, runs ExecStart as a new process, tracks its PID, logs to the journal, and restarts it if Restart= is set
  • start vs enable → now vs at boot | enable creates a symlink in the .wants folder
  • Service won't start after reboot → is-enabled (enabled?) → status → journalctl -u → path/permissions
  • Edited a unit file and nothing changed → forgot daemon-reload

docs.title: vi / vim
docs.text: From The Linux Command Line, chapter 12

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Always installed on servers → nano may not be → must be able to edit a config and exit
  • vi = original | vim = improved vi → on Ubuntu, vi opens vim

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• Normal (command) mode → default on open → keys are commands, not text
  • Insert mode → i → type text → Esc → back to normal
  • Command-line mode → : from normal → :w, :q etc.
  • Lost? → press Esc twice → you're in normal mode

docs.title: Open + Save + Quit
docs.text:
• vim file.txt → open/create
  • :w → save | :q → quit | :wq or :x or ZZ → save + quit
  • :q! → quit without saving (discard changes)
  • :w newname → save as

docs.title: Enter Insert Mode
docs.text:
• i → insert before cursor | a → after cursor
  • I → start of line | A → end of line
  • o → new line below | O → new line above

docs.title: Move (normal mode)
docs.text:
• h j k l → left down up right (arrow keys also work)
  • w → next word | b → back a word
  • 0 → start of line | $ → end of line
  • gg → first line | G → last line | 25G or :25 → go to line 25

docs.title: Edit (normal mode)
docs.text:
• x → delete char | dd → delete (cut) line | 3dd → 3 lines
  • dw → delete word | D → delete to end of line
  • yy → copy (yank) line | p → paste below | P → paste above
  • u → undo | Ctrl-r → redo
  • . → repeat last change

docs.title: Search + Replace
docs.text:
• /word → search forward | n → next | N → previous
  • :%s/old/new/g → replace all in file
  • :%s/old/new/gc → replace all, confirm each

docs.title: Useful
docs.text:
• :set number → line numbers | :set nonumber → off
  • vim +25 file → open at line 25 (from error messages)
  • sudo vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config → edit system files as root
  • E45: 'readonly' option is set → opened without sudo → :q! and reopen with sudo

Interview points

  • How to exit vim without saving → Esc then :q!
  • Edit a config on a server with no nano → vim, i, edit, Esc, :wq

docs.title: Working with Commands
docs.text:
From The Linux Command Line, chapter 5

  • Command → An instruction given to the shell to perform an operation.

docs.title: 4 kinds of commands
docs.text:
• Executable → a file on disk (mv → /usr/bin/mv)
  • Builtin → part of bash itself, no file (cd, type, alias, help)
  • Alias → a shortcut (ls → ls --color=auto)
  • Function → a small script loaded into the shell

docs.title: Finding Commands
docs.text:
• type command → Shows what kind of command it is (works for all 4). Best tool.
    • type cd → cd is a shell builtin
    • type ls → ls is aliased to 'ls --color=auto'
  • type -a command → Shows every match (alias, builtin and file), in the order bash checks them.
  • which command → Path of the executable being used.
    • which python3 → /usr/bin/python3
    • Prints nothing for builtins (cd, alias); they have no file.
    • Real use: "wrong version running" problems (which terraform, which kubectl).
  • command -v command → Like which, but also works for builtins and aliases (use this in scripts).
  • whereis command → Binary, source, and man page locations.
  • If both a builtin and a file exist (pwd), the builtin wins.
  • Bash looks in this order → alias → function → builtin → executable in $PATH.
  • echo $PATH → Directories searched for executables, left to right.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
• man command → Full manual page. (/word to search, n next match, q to quit)
  • command --help → Short usage/help message.
  • help command → Help for builtins only (help cd); fails for programs like find.
  • tldr command → Short practical examples (fastest).
  • man -k keyword → Search all manuals by keyword (= apropos).
  • whatis command → One-line description.

docs.title: Command History (ch 8)
docs.text:
• history → Previously executed commands.
  • history | grep docker → Find old commands containing a word.
  • ↑ / ↓ → Navigate history.
  • Ctrl + R → Reverse-search history.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
• alias ll='ls -la' → Creates a shortcut (lost when the terminal closes).
  • alias → Lists current aliases.
  • unalias ll → Removes an alias.
  • Permanent → add the line to ~/.bashrc, then source ~/.bashrc.
    • e.g. alias k=kubectl, alias tf=terraform
  • \ls → Runs the real command, skipping the alias.

Interview points

  • type vs which → type knows aliases/builtins/functions; which only finds files in $PATH.
  • "Command not found" → check echo $PATH, which cmd, whether it's installed, and whether you need ./ for a file in the current directory.
  • "Wrong version runs" → type -a cmd shows every match; the first one wins.
